objectives: Recognise repeated -at and -ap CVC spelling and sound patterns.
Compare CVC words by identifying the phoneme that changes.
Use a familiar word-family pattern as a decoding support while still reading every grapheme.
concepts: A word family contains words sharing a common ending pattern.
Changing one phoneme can create a new word.
Patterns support decoding but should not replace grapheme-by-grapheme reading.

definitions.definition: A group of words that share a common ending sound and spelling pattern.
Reading text or word sets that mainly use sound-spelling patterns already taught.

commonMistakes: Guessing a word from the family without checking its first or final sound.
Treating rhyming words as identical words.
revisionPoints: Pattern is a support, not a substitute for decoding.

conceptual: Identify the shared pattern and changing phoneme.
application: Build a new CVC word by changing one known sound.
higherOrderThinking: Explain why a word-family pattern can support but cannot replace decoding.
mixedReview: Decode, compare, classify and reread CVC word families.

formulaOrFactBank: Word family = shared ending sound + spelling pattern
mistakeBasedRevision: If two words are confused, isolate the differing phoneme and reread both words.
weakTopicRevision: Sort familiar CVC cards into -at and -ap families, then decode each card aloud.

activities.name: Change one sound
steps: Change the first sound to make sat.
Change it again to make pat.

activities.name: Controlled word reading
steps: Read a short set from one family.

outcomes: Learner accurately classifies at least 8 of 10 familiar CVC words into taught word families.
Learner identifies the changing phoneme when two related CVC words are compared.
Learner uses a repeated pattern as decoding support while checking every grapheme.

questions.question: Which word belongs to the -at family?
Which word belongs to the -ap family?
Which pair belongs to the same word family?
What stays the same in mat and sat?
What changes in mat → sat?
options: The first sound and first letter

questions.question: Which word completes the -at family: m-at, s-at, t-at?
Which word completes the -ap family: m-ap, t-ap?
Why are word families useful?
options: They help learners notice repeated sound and spelling patterns
They allow learners to guess every word
They remove the need to decode

questions.question: A learner sees 'sat'. What should they do first?
options: Look at the letters and say the sounds

questions.question: Which pair differs only in the first sound?
Which pair differs only in the final sound?
Which reading practice is best for a new word-family pattern?
options: Decode each word, then reread the set smoothly
Memorise the whole list without looking at sounds

questions.question: If a learner reads 'map' as 'mat', which part needs checking?
What is the safest way to use a familiar word family when reading a new word?
options: Use the pattern as a clue, then decode all graphemes
